ADMINISTRATOR’S FINAL ORDER
Liquor License No. LC-33376
NOW, on this 24th day of December 2014, this matter comes before the Administrator of the
Alcoholic Beverages Division (Division) on the Notice of Appeal filed by DTW, Inc., d/b/a
T.C.B. and Cream, LLC, d/b/a Union Bar, The (Licensees).
STATEMENT OF CASE
The Licensees filed a timely appeal of the proposed decision by an administrative law judge
(ALJ). That decision affirmed the Licensees were in violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h).
The basis for the ALJ decision was that the preponderance of the evidence established that
employees of The Union Bar and T.C.B. failed to exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether
Melissa Vega was under the legal age when they failed to carefully review her Iowa Instruction
Permit that established her age as 19.
In an Order dated July 11, 2014, the Administrator granted the Licensees’ request for review and
established a schedule for the parties to file objections or exceptions and present briefs in support
of their respective positions. The objections or exceptions and briefs of the appealing party were
due on or before Monday, August 11, 2014, and responsive briefs were due on or before
Wednesday, September 10, 2014. The record reflects that all briefs were timely filed by the
parties.
On appeal, the Licensees argue that the ALJ proposed decision to uphold the violations of Iowa
Code § 123.49(2)(h) were not supported by substantial evidence. The Licensees maintain that
when the evidence presented at hearing is considered as a whole, it shows that employees of The
1

Union Bar and T.C.B. did take reasonable care to ascertain the age of Ms. Vega. The Licensees
further argue that the violations should be dismissed because the original ID was not retained and
presented as evidence at hearing.
FINDINGS OF FACT
The findings of fact in the ALJ proposed decision are adopted and incorporated into this ruling as
if set out in full.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
The conclusions of law in the ALJ proposed decision are adopted and incorporated into this
ruling as if set out in full.
BASIS FOR DECISION
The Licensees claim that employees of The Union Bar and T.C.B. did exercise reasonable care to
ascertain the age of Ms. Vega when they carefully examined Ms. Vega’s instruction permit and
denied entry of “K” into their establishments. The burden of proving compliance with the statute
is on the licensee. McCrea v. Iowa Department of Transportation, 336 N.W.2d 427 (Iowa 1983).
Evidence presented at hearing shows that Mr. Garcia, the doorperson for The Union Bar, and Mr.
Smith, the doorperson for T.C.B., asked for and reviewed Ms. Vega’s instruction permit prior to
her entry into each establishment. According to testimony, Mr. Smith looked at the date of birth
and verified that Ms. Vega was the person pictured on the ID; while Mr. Garcia looked at the
date of birth, saw the state seal and reviewed the picture to confirm that Ms. Vega was the person
pictured on the ID. It appears that Mr. Garcia and Mr. Smith relied solely on the date of birth
printed on the instruction permit to calculate Ms. Vega’s age to determine if she was of legal age.
The Division has consistently held that the reasonable care standard requires more than just
requesting an ID. Licensees and their employees must thoroughly examine the purchaser’s ID to
verify that the person is the person pictured on the ID and that they are of legal age. However,
the actions of the Licensees doorpersons fell short of a careful examination of the ID. The ID
was vertical in orientation and titled “IOWA INSTRUCTION PERMIT", which should have
caused the Licensees to be more vigilant of Ms. Vega’s age. Moreover, just above the date of
birth is a red band with wording “UNDER 18 UNTIL 11/5/2011”. A careful review of the entire
ID for age verification would have shown that Ms. Vega was not of legal age.
The Licensees assert the violations be dismissed due to the original ID not being retained and
presented as evidence at hearing. However, Iowa Code § 17A.14 allows documentary evidence
to be received in the form of copies or excerpts, if the original is not readily available. The ALJ
thoroughly and accurately details the reasons for relying on the photocopy of the ID while
dismissing the Licensees assertions that the ID was not discernable.
The misfortune of misreading the date of birth does not excuse the responsibility of the
Licensees. A miscalculation or careless review of a driver’s license constitutes a failure to
2

exercise reasonable care. Motif, Ltd., d/b/a Bo-James v. Iowa Department of Commerce
Alcoholic Beverages Division No. 11-0328, 2011 WL 4378166 (Iowa App. 2011).
When Licensees challenge an administrative action and fail to produce supporting evidence to
satisfy the Licensees’ burden of proof, the decision should be affirmed. Gaskey v. Iowa
Department of Transportation, 537 N.W. 2d 695 (Iowa 1995). The preponderance of the
evidence demonstrates that the doorpersons did not exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether
Ms. Vega was of the legal age on November 16, 2012. As a direct result of the failure to
exercise reasonable care, the bartenders sold beer to Ms. Vega. Each employee’s failure to
exercise reasonable care is deemed to be the act of the Licensees and subjects the Licensees to
applicable penalties. Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(a) mandates a five hundred dollar ($500.00) civil
penalty for a first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h).
ORDER
The decision of the administrative law judge is supported by the record and hereby affirmed.
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED that liquor license number LC0033376, issued to Cream,
LLC, d/b/a Union Bar, The, 121 E. College St., Iowa City, Iowa, pay a civil penalty of five
hundred dollars ($500.00) for a first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). The civil penalty is
due and payable to the “Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division,” 1918 SE Hulsizer Road, Ankeny,
Iowa 50021, on or before January 23, 2015. Failure to timely pay the civil penalty shall result in
further administrative proceedings.
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that liquor license number LC0036265, issued to DTW, Inc.,
d/b/a T.C.B., 114 E. College St., Iowa City, Iowa, pay a civil penalty of five hundred dollars
($500.00) for a first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). The civil penalty is due and payable
to the “Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division,” 1918 SE Hulsizer Road, Ankeny, Iowa 50021, on
or before January 23, 2015. Failure to timely pay the civil penalty shall result in further
administrative proceedings.
The parties are hereby notified that pursuant to Iowa Code § 17A.19, this Order constitutes final
agency action for the purpose of Iowa Code chapters 17A and 123. This Order becomes final,
unless a party to the hearing files a Petition for Judicial Review with the Iowa District Court
within 30 days from the date of this Order.
Moreover, the parties are notified that pursuant to Iowa Code § 17A.19(5), the filing of a petition
for judicial review does not automatically stay execution or enforcement of the Division’s action.
The Division may grant a stay on appropriate terms or other temporary remedies during the
pendency of judicial review. If the Division refuses to grant the stay or other temporary
remedies, the court may grant the relief.

On September 9, 2013, the Iowa Department of Public Safety (DPS) filed an
administrative hearing complaint against Cream LLC, d/b/a The Union Bar
(licensee). On September 10, 2013, DPS filed an administrative hearing
complaint against DTW, Inc., d/b/a T.C.B. (licensee). The two hearing complaints
both alleged that on November 16, 2012, the licensee or an employee of the
licensee sold or supplied an alcoholic beverage, wine, or beer to a person under
the legal age, in violation of Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h).
On October 15, 2013, DPS filed an Unresisted Motion for Continuance and for
Consolidation of Hearings. Both motions were granted.1 A consolidated hearing
was held before the undersigned administrative law judge on May 9, 2014 at the
office of the Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals, Administrative
1 This consolidated case initially also included a third case, Docket No. D-2013-00121, which has
was informally resolved when the business was sold and a new liquor license was issued. (Order
Consolidating Three Cases; Testimony of Annie Adamovicz)

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 2
Hearings Division, Wallace State Office Building-Third Floor, Des Moines, Iowa.
Assistant Attorney General John Lundquist represented DPS. The licensees
were both represented by attorney Joseph Moreland.
THE RECORD
The record includes the two Hearing Complaints; Initial Notices of Hearing;
Unresisted Motion for Continuance and Consolidation; Order Consolidating
Three Cases for Hearing and Continuance Order; two additional Continuance
Orders; and a Subpoena to Appear issued to Melissa Vega. The record also
includes the testimony of Melissa Vega (by telephone), Annie Adamovicz, Jeff
Maynes, Jesse Garcia, Christopher Smith (by telephone), and Kurt LeClere. The
record also includes DPS Exhibits 1-11 (See Exhibit Index for description),
Respondent Exhibits A-B, and the professional statements of attorneys Joseph
Moreland and John Lundquist.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Undercover Alcohol Compliance Check on November 16, 2012
Facts Common to Both Cases
On November 16, 2012, the Iowa City Police Department conducted an
undercover alcohol compliance check of licensed liquor establishments in Iowa
City, Iowa. Melissa Vega, a full-time student at Kirkwood Community College,
volunteered to participate in the compliance check after receiving information
about the opportunity from her criminal justice professor. Ms. Vega was born on
November 5, 1993 and was 19 years old on November 16, 2012. Iowa City Police
Officer Paul Batcheller contacted Ms. Vega a few days before the compliance
check and then met with her on the day of the compliance check. A second
underage female (K) also participated in alcohol compliance checks that same
day. Ms. Vega and K went to some of the establishments together on November
16, 2012. (Testimony of Melissa Vega; DPS Exhibits 1, 2, 5)
This was the first time that Melissa Vega had ever participated in an undercover
alcohol compliance check, but she did participate in additional undercover
compliance checks with the Iowa City Police Department after November 16,
2012. Ms. Vega cannot recall exactly how many establishments she visited as
part of the November 16, 2012 compliance check, nor could she recall how many
of the establishments sold alcohol to her. At hearing, Ms. Vega estimated that

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 3
the number of establishments she visited on November 16, 2012 was in the “high
twenties” and that most of the establishments refused to serve her. (Testimony
of Melissa Vega; DPS Exhibits 1, 2, 5)
Following a compliance check, the Iowa City Police Department emails copies of
its investigation reports and any resulting citations to the Iowa Alcoholic
Beverages Division (Division). Annie Adamovicz is an Administrative Assistant
employed by the Division, and her duties include receiving law enforcement
reports and complaints and setting hearing dates. Following the November 16,
2012 compliance check, Ms. Adamovicz received investigation reports and
citations (including DPS Exhibits 1, 2, 4, 5, and 7) from the Iowa City Police
Department. The documents that Ms. Adamovicz received indicated that six
licensed liquor establishments, including the three cases that were initially
consolidated as part of this appeal, failed the alcohol compliance check
conducted on November 16, 2012. Ms. Adamovicz could not attest to the
accuracy of the investigation reports and citations and did not know the total
number of establishments that were checked in Iowa City that day. (Testimony
of Annie Adamovicz; DPS Exhibits 1, 2, 4, 5, 7)
None of the Iowa City police officers who participated in the alcohol compliance
check appeared to testify at hearing. The Incident Reports prepared by the
officers were admitted as exhibits, and DPS called Ms. Vega as its only witness.2
Ms. Vega testified that she and K were searched prior to the compliance checks
and were only allowed to carry their phones, their identification cards (IDs), and
money provided by the police department to make alcohol purchases. The
Incident Reports also state that Ms. Vega was thoroughly searched and only
possessed an ID that showed her to be under 21. (Testimony of Melissa Vega;
DPS Exhibits 1, 5)
Melissa Vega further testified that she and K were told “not to be sneaky,” and to
give their actual age if they were asked for their ages. At the end of the evening,
Ms. Vega wrote Voluntary Statements for each alcohol purchase that she made,
including the two at issue in this proceeding. The Voluntary Statements were
signed by Ms. Vega. (Testimony of Melissa Vega; DPS Exhibits 3, 6)
2 The licensee’s attorney objected to DPS calling Ms. Vega as its own witness because the licensee
had subpoenaed her after being informed that DPS was not planning to call her as a witness.
This objection was overruled because the parties had not made any formal discovery requests
and had only informally exchanged information about their planned witnesses and exhibits.

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 4
On November 16, 2012, Melissa Vega did not yet have an Iowa driver’s license.
Ms. Vega had a state-issued Iowa Instruction Permit that was similar in
appearance to a driver’s license, with some exceptions. Ms. Vega’s Iowa
Instruction Permit had a vertical format3 and the words “Iowa Instruction
Permit” at the very top. It had the state seal and included two photographs of
Ms. Vega; her date of birth, her sex, height, and eye color; her address; the dates
of issuance and expiration, and restrictions. Ms. Vega’s date of birth is
superimposed over a second, smaller photograph of her, and the numbers in her
date of birth are red in color. There was also a red band to the right of Ms.
Vega’s larger photograph and just above her second smaller photograph. There
is yellow printing on the red band that states “Under 18 Until 11/5/2011.”
(Testimony of Melissa Vega; DPS Exhibits 8, 9; Licensee Exhibits A and B)
Prior to the compliance check, Melissa Vega did not tell the Iowa City Police
Department that she did not have a driver’s license and only had an Iowa
Instruction Permit. Ms. Vega does not recall having any discussion with the
officers about her Instruction Permit nor does she recall any discussion with the
officers about the legibility of the birth date on her Instruction Permit. Ms. Vega
recalled that someone took a photograph of her Instruction Permit using either a
cellphone or a camera, and she identified DPS Exhibit 8 as an accurate depiction
of her Iowa Instruction Permit. Ms. Vega did not think that her Instruction
Permit was difficult to read, although she conceded that some of the digits in her
birthdate (the 5 and the 3) are more difficult to read than the other digits because
they are printed over the black collar of the coat that she was wearing when the
photo was taken for the ID. (Testimony of Melissa Vega; DPS Exhibit 8)
On November 19, 2012 (three days after the compliance check), Melissa Vega
turned in her Iowa Instruction Permit to the Iowa Department of Transportation
and obtained an Iowa Driver’s License, which also has a vertical format. Ms.
Vega testified that she decided to get her driver’s license because her parents had
finally agreed to allow her to have a car at school and her sister was going to get
her driver’s license on the same day. Ms. Vega denies that her participation in
the undercover compliance check had any bearing on the timing of her decision
to get her driver’s license. The Iowa City Police Department told Ms. Vega that
she may be called as a witness concerning the compliance check, but they never
3 The vertical license format means that the person was underage at the time the license was
issued but does not necessarily mean that the person is still underage. A vertical format is a
recognized cue for persons checking the license to take a closer look to be sure the person is of
legal age. (Testimony of Jeff Maynes; Christopher Smith; Kurt LeClere.)

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 5
told her to retain her Iowa Instruction Permit. Ms. Vega used her Iowa Driver’s
license when she participated in additional undercover compliance checks after
November 19, 2012. (Testimony of Melissa Vega; DPS Exhibit 9)
Compliance Check at Cream LLC, d/b/a The Union Bar
Cream, LLC, d/b/a The Union Bar is a licensed liquor establishment (Liquor
License LC-33376) located at 121 E. College Street in Iowa City, Iowa. Jeff
Maynes is a member of Cream, LLC and has been one of the owners of The
Union Bar since 2007. All of The Union Bar’s employees have received formal
training concerning alcoholic beverage sales, including specific training on
preventing sales to underage persons and spotting fake IDs. The training has
been obtained through the TIPS or the I-PACT training programs. (Testimony
of Jeff Maynes; DPS Exhibit 10).
On November 16, 2012 at approximately 10:20 p.m., Melissa Vega and K went to
The Union Bar accompanied by police officers Adam Schmerbach and Brad
Murphy. The Union Bar uses a doorperson to check the identification of all
patrons and to place wristbands on patrons who are over 21. Bartenders are not
expected to recheck the identification of patrons wearing wrist bands. Union Bar
employee Jesse Garcia was employed as the doorperson that evening. Mr. Garcia
is 26 years old and has been employed by The Union Bar for approximately five
years. He has been a doorperson for three years and was a security guard for
two years before that. Mr. Garcia received on-the-job training to be a doorman
and had also been TIPS trained prior to November 16, 2012. Mr. Garcia also
received I-PACT training after November 16, 2012. (DPS Exhibits 1, 2;
Testimony of Melissa Vega, Jeff Maynes, Jesse Garcia)
When working as a doorperson, Jesse Garcia stands outside The Union Bar
entrance and requires all patrons to show identification, regardless of their age.
He uses the street light and the flood light on the building to help him read the
information on the patron’s ID. The first thing he looks at is the date of birth,
and the second thing he looks at is the person’s photograph to be sure that the
person in front of him is the person depicted on the ID. If he has difficulty
reading anything on the ID he may try holding the ID differently for a better
view, or he will ask for a second form of valid identification. (Testimony of Jesse
Garcia)

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 6
Jesse Garcia remembered Melissa Vega and K coming to The Union Bar on
November 16, 2012. He recalled that Melissa Vega was first in line. Mr. Garcia
looked at the birthdate on her ID, read her birth year as 1990, and calculated her
age as 22 years old. Mr. Garcia saw the state seal on the ID and reviewed the
photograph to confirm that it was in fact Ms. Vega’s ID. Mr. Garcia denies
having any difficulty reading the ID, and he testified that the last digit of the
birth year clearly appeared to him to be a “0.” Mr. Garcia further testified that
the glare on the IDs can sometimes make a “3” look like a “0.” Mr. Garcia did
not look at the red bar to the right of Vega’s photograph and did not see that it
said “Under 18 until 11/5/2011.” Mr. Garcia allowed Melissa Vega to enter The
Union Bar (Testimony of Jesse Garcia)
In her contemporaneous written statement and in her testimony at hearing,
Melissa Vega stated that she showed her ID to the doorperson at the Union Bar,
and he gave her a wrist band. Ms. Vega could not recall if K was with her when
she went to The Union Bar. (Testimony of Melissa Vega; DPS Exhibit 3)
The Incident Supplement prepared by Officer Brad Murphy indicates that both
Ms. Vega and K went to The Union Bar on November 16, 2012. Officer Murphy
indicated in his report that Jesse Garcia looked at both IDs, did not allow one girl
to enter, but gave the other girl a wristband and allowed her to enter the bar.
(DPS Exhibit 2)
Jesse Garcia recalled that K was behind Melissa Vega in line. He further recalled
that K’s identification had a birth date in 1994, which meant she was 20 years old.
After Mr. Garcia told K that she could not enter, Mr. Garcia recalled that K told
him “but you let my friend in.” Mr. Garcia reports that he responded “your
friend has a good ID.” At this point, Mr. Garcia did not know that Melissa Vega
and K were part of an undercover compliance check. (Testimony of Jesse Garcia)
After Melissa Vega entered the Union Bar she walked up to the bartender and
asked for a Bud Light beer. Ms. Vega knew that an officer was inside the
establishment watching her but could not recall the name of the officer. DPS
Exhibit 1 indicates that Officer Adam Schmerbach was inside The Union Bar and
witnessed the sale. The bartender, later identified as Tyler James Tiecker, served
Ms. Vega the beer and accepted payment from her without requesting any
identification from her. Following this transaction, Officer Adam Schmerbach
identified himself to Mr. Tiecker and told him that he had failed an alcohol
compliance check and would be getting a citation for serving a person under the

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 7
age of 21. Mr. Tiecker responded that bouncers check IDs at the front door and
the bartender does not check IDs of persons who have wrist bands. Mr. Tiecker
was issued a citation for selling alcohol to an underage person, in violation of
Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h). The citation was later dismissed by the court.
(Testimony of Melissa Vega; DPS Exhibits 1-4)
Jesse Garcia testified that a police officer approached him at his post outside the
bar, asked for his identification, and told him that he had not passed a
compliance check. Mr. Garcia reports that he asked the officer “you mean the ’94
girl? Because she didn’t get in.” (Testimony of Jesse Garcia)
In his Incident Supplement report, Officer Murphy acknowledges that he spoke
to Jesse Garcia and “ran his information” while the other officers issued a citation
to the bartender. Officer Murphy’s Incident Supplement report does not give
any details concerning the conversation between Mr. Garcia and Officer Murphy.
It further states that after Officer Murphy left the bar, he decided to go back and
ask Mr. Garcia a few more questions. When he returned to the bar, however, Mr.
Garcia had been sent home by management. (DPS Exhibit 2)
Jeff Maynes was present at The Union Bar on November 16, 2012. One of the
officers told him that they had failed a compliance check and had served a
person born in 1993. Mr. Maynes did not see Ms. Vega’s ID. Mr. Maynes sent
Jesse Garcia home. He later found out that Mr. Garcia thought the “3” on Ms.
Vega’s ID was a “0.” (Testimony of Jeff Maynes)
Compliance Check at DTW, Inc. d/b/a T.C.B.
DTW, Inc. d/b/a T.C.B. is a licensed liquor establishment (Liquor License LC-
36265) located at 114 E. College Street in Iowa City, Iowa. Kurt LeClere has
been a part owner of T.C.B. for the past six years. Mr. LeClere has been involved
in the bar business for 28 years and has been a bar owner for the past 16 years.
All of T.C.B.’s door persons have received formal training, through the TIPS or
the I-PACT training programs, as well as on-the-job training on preventing sales
to underage persons by properly checking IDs. Door persons are trained to look
at everything on the person’s ID, but the first thing that they are told to look at is
the person’s date of birth. (Testimony of Kurt LeClere; DPS Exhibit 11).
On November 16, 2012 at approximately 10:34 p.m., Melissa Vega went to T.C.B.
accompanied by police officer Adam Schmerbach. T.C.B. uses a doorperson to

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 8
check the identification of all patrons, and employee Christopher Smith was
employed as the doorperson that evening. Mr. Smith is currently 26 years old,
and he worked at T.C.B. for about 18 months before leaving to take a higher
paying job. Mr. Smith had been trained by Kurt LeClere, who watches the
doorpersons carefully to make sure they are doing their job correctly. Mr. Smith
also had TIPS training prior to November 16, 2012. At some point in time Mr.
Smith had I-PACT training. (DPS Exhibits 1, 2; Testimony of Melissa Vega,
Christopher Smith)
When checking identification at T.C.B., Christopher Smith would stand just
outside the entrance if the weather was nice or just inside the door in inclement
weather. There are overhead lights in the doorway to help doorpersons view IDs
and Mr. Smith also carried a flashlight which he nearly always used to view the

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
I. Statutory Prohibition of Sales to Underage Persons, the “Reasonable
Care to Ascertain” Standard, and Licensee’s Liability for Administrative
Sanctions Based on Employees’ Acts.
Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h)(2013) provides, in relevant part:
2. A person or club holding a liquor control license or retail
wine or beer permit under this chapter, and the person's or club's
agents or employees, shall not do any of the following:
...
h. Sell, give, or otherwise supply any alcoholic beverage, wine
or beer to any person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable
care to ascertain whether the person is under legal age, or permit
any person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to
ascertain whether the person is under legal age, to consume any
alcoholic beverage, wine, or beer.
The Iowa Code defines "legal age" as twenty-one years of age or more.4
A violation of Iowa Code chapter 123 by any employee, agent, or servant of a
licensee or permittee shall be deemed to be the act of the licensee or permittee
and shall subject the license to suspension or revocation.5
Iowa Code section 123.50 provides, in relevant part:
4 Iowa Code section 123.3(24)(2013).
5 185 IAC 4.8.

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 11
123.50 Criminal and civil penalties.
...
3. If any licensee, wine permittee, beer permittee, or employee
of a licensee or permittee is convicted or found in violation of
section 123.49, subsection 2, paragraph "h", the administrator or
local authority shall, in addition to criminal penalties fixed for
violations by this section, assess a civil penalty as follows:
a. A first violation shall subject the licensee or permittee to a
civil penalty in the amount of five hundred dollars. Failure to
pay the civil penalty as ordered under section 123.39 shall result in
automatic suspension of the license or permit for a period of
fourteen days.
(emphasis added).
A criminal conviction is not a prerequisite to suspension, revocation or
imposition of a civil penalty. 6 A license sanction may be based on a finding of
violation made following an administrative hearing.7
The Iowa Supreme Court has recognized that, at a very minimum, the exercise of
reasonable care to ascertain the age of a person, as required by Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h), requires a licensee’s employees to request identification from
patrons prior to selling alcohol to them unless their age is known or reasonably
beyond question.8 The Alcoholic Beverages Division has consistently held that
the reasonable care standard requires more than just requesting identification.
Licensees and their employees must carefully examine the customer’s photo
identification to verify that the person presenting the ID is in fact over the age of
21. A careless review of the identification is not reasonable care. 9
6 Iowa Code section 123.39(1)(c)(2013).
7 Iowa Code section 123.50(3)(2013).
8 Jim O. Inc. v. City of Cedar Rapids, 587 N.W.2d 476, 478 (Iowa 1998).
9 See, e.g. Administrator’s Final Decision in D-2010-00244, p.3, issued 6/29/11 (“The ABD has
consistently held that the reasonable care standard requires more than just requesting the
customer’s identification. A miscalculation or careless review of a driver’s license constitutes a
failure to exercise reasonable care.”)

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 12
In an administrative enforcement proceeding against a licensee for selling
alcohol to an underage person, it is irrelevant if the licensee divides the duties of
checking identification and serving alcohol between two different employees or
if a single employee checks identification and serves alcohol. The licensee is
still responsible for administrative sanctions when alcohol is sold to an underage
customer if the employee responsible for checking the customer’s identification
fails to do so or does so carelessly.10
II. Analysis
The preponderance of the evidence in this record established that on November
16, 2012, the doorpersons employed by The Union Bar and T.C.B. (licensees)
refused entry to one underage female (K) participating in the compliance check
but allowed the second female, 19 year old Melissa Vega, to enter their licensed
establishments. In both cases, the doorperson asked Melissa Vega for
identification and examined the Iowa Instruction Permit that she presented
before allowing her to enter the bar. Bartenders employed by both licensees
then sold beer to Ms. Vega, and the sales were witnessed by undercover police
officers.
The sole issue is whether or not the two doorpersons exercised reasonable care to
ascertain whether Melissa Vega was under the legal age to purchase and
consume alcohol. It is undisputed that Ms. Vega’s birth date is 11/5/1993 and
that she was 19 years old at the time of the compliance check. Both doorpersons
looked at Ms. Vega’s photograph to make sure that the ID belonged to her and
both looked at her date of birth, which appeared in red just to the right of her
photograph. Both doorpersons testified that they read the last digit of Ms.
Vega’s birthdate on her Iowa Instruction Permit as a “0” and not as a “3.”
Moreover, both doorpersons claim that the last digit clearly appeared to be a “0”
and therefore they did not consider looking at the red banner above her
photograph, which stated “Under 18 until 11/5/2011.”
10 See Motif, LTD, Bo-James v. Iowa Dep’t of Commerce-Alcoholic Beverages Division, 807 N.W.2d 158,
2011 WL 4378166 (Table in Westlaw, Unpublished Disposition, Iowa App., Sept. 21,
2011)(holding licensee liable for sale to underage person when bartender relied on doorperson to
check identification and the doorperson did so carelessly, even though evidence supported the
finding that the licensee took care to train its employees, and the doorperson was generally
conscientious).

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 13
The preponderance of the evidence in the record supports the conclusion that
both doorpersons failed to exercise reasonable care when they examined Ms.
Vega’s Iowa Instruction Permit and concluded that she was over the legal age.
A reasonable person faced with these same circumstances would have subjected
Ms. Vega’s ID to careful scrutiny. The ID she presented was an Instruction
Permit with a vertical format. Although this does not mean that she was in fact
underage, both of these readily observable features on the ID should have alerted
the doorpersons that the ID required careful examination.
Both doorpersons looked only at the date of birth and the photograph on the ID.
Both claim that the last digit of the birthdate clearly appeared to them to be a “0.”
Given their claims, it is unfortunate that the original Instruction Permit is not
available for examination. Ms. Vega’s explanation about the timing of her
decision to get a driver’s license and the surrender of her Instruction Permit to
the Department of Transportation was entirely plausible and credible, however.
There is no basis in this record to conclude that there was any improper motive
behind Ms. Vega’s decision to surrender her Instruction Permit and obtain a
driver’s license.
It is typical for officers take a photograph or to make a copy of the ID used by the
underage person in a compliance check, and a photograph was taken of Ms.
Vega’s Instruction Permit in this case. It is also typical for photocopies or
photographs of IDs to be submitted as evidence in administrative sanction
hearings concerning compliance checks. A photocopy or a photograph of
anything may be less clear or crisp than the original. The quality of the copy
machine, cell phone, or camera and the care and skill of the person using the
equipment can all affect the quality of the resulting image. In addition, when a
digital photograph is printed, the quality of the resulting image can also be
affected by the quality of the printer that is used. It is highly unlikely, however,
that the quality of the printer or an adjustment of the printer’s lighting could add
any detail that was not present in the original photograph or in the original ID.
The record includes three printed copies of the photograph taken of Melissa
Vega’s instruction permit: DPS Exhibit 8 and Licensee Exhibits A and B. The
right side of the photographs in Exhibits A and B are substantially darker than
the right side of the photograph in DPS Exhibit 8. In all three exhibits, the last
digit of Ms. Vega’s birthdate is at least somewhat obscured because it is printed
over the dark collar of her coat. The last digit of the birthdate does not appear to
be a “0” in any of the three exhibits. The last digit is not legible at all in Exhibits

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 14
A and B. In DPS Exhibit 8, however, the last digit of Ms. Vega’s birthdate is
legible as a “3.” The center line on the three is not completely faded, as claimed
by Christopher Smith. The left side of the 3 is open and is not a complete circle,
as it would be if it was a “0.” These exhibits do not support the doorpersons’
claims that the “3” clearly appeared as a “0” on the original Instruction Permit.
In addition, many other establishments refused service to Ms. Vega, which was
also inconsistent with the claims made by Mr. Garcia and Mr. Smith that the “3”
clearly appeared to be a “0” on the original Instruction Permit.
If the last digit of Ms. Vega’s birthdate on her Instruction Permit was unclear or
difficult to read, a doorperson who was exercising reasonable care to determine
her age would look at the information on red band above her birthdate to verify
her age. Even in the poor quality copy submitted by the licensees (Exhibit A), the
writing on the red band is clearly legible as stating that Ms. Vega will be under
18 until 2011. The preponderance of the evidence established that employees of
The Union Bar and T.C.B. failed to exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether
Melissa Vega was under the legal age when they failed to carefully review her
Iowa Instruction Permit that established her age as 19. As a result, Ms. Vega
was served beer in both establishments, in violation of Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h).
